As discussed by Nicholas Parrillo, one possible remedy for the threat that 
guidance may pose to the APA’s safeguards on regulatory power “is to change 
the process by which guidance gets issued in the first place, to make it more 
participatory.” ParriUo explains:
*    These [process reforms] can involve a little participation or 
a lot, up to and including “voluntary notice-and-comment,” in which 
the agency does something similar to what it does for a legislative 
rule—publish the guidance document in draft and invite the public to 
send its reactions—^though more streambnod (e.g., ofFering little or 
no response to the comments, or building less of a record).
** *
*   The most influential real-world experiment with such 
participation has been    the FDA Good Guidance Practices 
(GGPs), a set of procedural rules initially adopted by the agency in 
early 1997, specifically authorized and required by Congress later 
that year, and then repromulgated, without fundamental changes, 
in 2000.1'1 Under the GGPs, the FDA conducts notice-and-comment 
prior to the adoption of all ‘Tjevel 1” guidance documents, defined by 
an elaborate provision that encompasses basically any guidance of 
consequence.
* *
* * *
Using the FDA “as a model,” the Office of Management and 
Budget (0MB) during the George AV. Bush adroinistration adopted 
its own version of Good Guidance Practices to be followed by all 
executive agencies.i® In particular, 0MB told executive agencies to 
conduct notice-and-comment before adopting any “ppn-nnrnirally 
significant” guidance document.i« This did not go as far as the FDA, 
because OMB’s mandate for “economically significant” guidance 
covered a category of documents that (while loosely defined) was 
obviously narrower than that for which the FDA took public
